messages.subject: Measurement invariance with three groups
messages.subject_clean: Measurement invariance with three groups
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
I am relatively new to lavaan and SEM, and I would like to ask you for some advice. I am trying to evaluate measurement invariance of an instrument (four factor, 22 continuous items) across three different groups. My doubts are as follows:

1. Following the lavaan tutorial, with equality constraints in place for factor loadings and item intercepts, I am fixing the latent mean of each factor to zero in the first group (G1, reference group), whereas these means are freely estimated in the other two groups (G2 and G3). Can I interpret the latent means of G2 and G3 in each factor as differences between G2 vs G1, and G3 vs G1, respectively, as in the case of an analysis with two groups?

2. How about a post-hoc analysis of latent mean differences between G2 and G3?

3. I have some missing values. Is it possible to use full-information maximum likelihood together with the MLR estimator in the framework of measurement invariance?

Thank you very much for your help.

All the best

Marika

messages.subject: Re: Measurement invariance with three groups
messages.subject_clean: Measurement invariance with three groups
messages.body_plain:
Marika

####

1. Following the lavaan tutorial, with equality constraints in place for factor loadings and item intercepts, I am fixing the latent mean of each factor to zero in the first group (G1, reference group), whereas these means are freely estimated in the other two groups (G2 and G3). Can I interpret the latent means of G2 and G3 in each factor as differences between G2 vs G1, and G3 vs G1, respectively, as in the case of an analysis with two groups?

####
For this to hold you need to achieve strong measurement invariance, meaning that both factor loadings and indicator intercepts can be equated between groups.
Once you have achieve this, yes, the means for g2 and g3 would be the difference with respect of G1, because its set to 0
You can also use the function measEq.syntax() from the semTools package to create the models syntax for these steps, in case you are not clear

####

2. How about a post-hoc analysis of latent mean differences between G2 and G3?

####

messages.body_plain:
Marika

I dont know a paper that specifically talks about this mean difference, because there is no dispute about it.

The mean of G2 and G3 are not by definition the difference with respect of G1. Their means are estimated with G1 as the point of reference. They represent the difference because G1 is fix at 0, you could fix it 10 if you want and G2 and G3 would change accordingly, in refernece to it

Even when G2 and G3 are the difference with G1, the effect of G1 "cancels out" when comparing G2 and G3. Because if both have G1 as the same reference point, their difference (G2 - G3) is still the difference that is not related to the difference with G1. Think like you are adding a constant to both sides of the substraction, the final substraction will result in the same (G2-0) - (G3-0)

Hope this helps

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am fitting an SEM to simulated data consisting of 10000
observations of 5 observed variables. Each latent factor in the model has a
single indicator and the error variance of the indicator is predetermined using
the reliability of each observed variable.

My question relates to the relationship between mean
centering and accounting for missingness using full-information maximum
likelihood. If I ignore missingness, as expected the model fit and model
results are identical on both raw data and on mean-centered data (the same data
set with each variable centered on zero, using R’s scale(dat, center=T,
scale=F)).

However, if some observations are removed from the data set
and the same model refitted using missing=”fiml”, then the version
without mean-centering yields different standardised loadings, different
exogenous latent variances, and a chi-squared statistic of the order of 10000
times larger. Why does mean-centering make such a difference in the case where
there is missing data, or is this something to do with the treatment of “fiml”
under the hood? I’d really appreciate an explanation of what is going on and
what I can do about it!

The model and some output:

mod <-   "
f1 =~ 1*x1                                                 #
single indicator loadings fixed at 1

              f2 =~ 1*x2

              f3 =~ 1*x3

              f4 =~ 1*x4

              f5 =~ 1*x5

              f2 ~ f1                                                                #
structural model

messages.body_plain:
Dear Lavaan group,

I am working on a confirmatory factor analysis in a dataset with 15 items (possible answer: 1 or 0) and some missing values. I suppose that there is an one underlying latent variable among these. I define the ordered variables and my model as:

model <- '

g =~ A1 + A2+A3+ A4 + A5+A6+A7+A8+ A9+A10+ A11+A12+A13+A14+ A15

'

then I fit the model:

gfit <- cfa(model, data=dataSEM, ordered=ordered, missing="pairwise",estimator = "WLSMV", std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE)

summary(gfit,  fit.measures=TRUE)

dataSEM$score <- lavPredict(gfit, type = "lv")

The focus is to extract the “prediction” of the latent variable g.

Is the model fitted in the right way? I need to parametrize ‘theta’?  how can I interpret the coefficient (e.g A1 on g)? via the identity function?

If I add a binary measured outcome (Y) in this way:

model <- '

g =~ A1 + A2+A3+ A4 + A5+A6+A7+A8+ A9+A10+ A11+A12+A13+A14+ A15

Y~ g+X1

'

The interpretation of coefficient refers on Y is via probit?

Thanks a lot for your help J

Francesca

messages.body_plain:
Dear Lavaan group,

Help is needed.

I carry out a CFA with categorical data using a data with missing values. My approach, however, seems to run into issues that previous posts do not seem to address. Following the previous suggestions, I prepared the analysis in R as follows:

install.packages("lavaan", repos = "http://www.da.ugent.be", type = "source")
install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("simsem/semTools/semTools")

I also downloaded and installed Rtools 3.5 to make sure all is in place. So I should have amongst others the development version of lavaan in place. In order to generate the imputations, I have been using MICE (EXCLUDE is a set of variables I did not want to use for the imputations):

PREDICTORMATRIX <- quickpred(BASELINE, exclude = EXCLUDE, mincor = 0.2, method = "kendall")
IMPUTE <- mice(BASELINE, predictorMatrix = PREDICTORMATRIX, m = 5)

I want to test various models all looped through the cfa command. One of the simpler models is of the form

MODELS$M1 <- '
C_Mot =~ 1* C_AB2+ C_AB3+ C_AB4+ C_AB5 + C_AB6 + C_AB8 + C_AB_PO2
E_Motivation =~ 1*E_AB2+ E_AB3+ E_AB4+ E_AB5 + E_AB6 + E_AB8
K_Motivation =~ 1* K_AB2+ K_AB3+ K_AB4+ K_AB5 + K_AB6 + K_AB8
M_Motivation =~ 1* M_AB2+ M_AB3+ M_AB4+ M_AB5 + M_AB6 + M_AB8 + M_AB_PO2'

The different models are saved in the list called MODELS. Since the I have multiply imputed data sets, I use runIM. In the loop below, all analysis output will be saved in the list called fits. VARIABLES specifies the categorical variables in the model (e.g. C_AB2).

for (MOD in 1: length(MODELS)) {
  fits$fit <- runMI(MODELS[[MOD]],
                    data=IMPUTE,
                    fun="cfa",
                    ordered= VARIABLES)
  names(fits)[length(fits)] <- paste0("M",MOD)
}

Without imputations, this general set up (e.g. loop) seems to have worked fine. With the imputations, however, I nw run into problems. The loop spits out the following error message:

"D3" only available using maximum likelihood estimation. Changed test to "D2".
Robust corrections are made by pooling the naive chi-squared statistic across 5 imputations for which the model converged, then applying the average (across imputations) scaling factor and shift parameter to that pooled value.
To instead pool the robust test statistics, set test = "D2" and pool.robust = TRUE.

and

Error in getMethod("resid", "lavaan.mi") :
  no method found for function 'resid' and signature lavaan.mi
In addition: Warning messages:
  1: In pchisq(X2, DF, ncp = N * DF * 0.05^2/nG, lower.tail = FALSE) :
  full precision may not have been achieved in 'pnchisq'
2: In pchisq(X2.sc, DF, ncp = N * DF * 0.05^2/nG, lower.tail = FALSE) :
  full precision may not have been achieved in 'pnchisq'

The first error message has continued to emerge for seevral iterations of my attempts to make it work. In fact, it made me look up solutions in this group amongst others. The second one is rather new and I could not find anything about it. Any help much appreciated. I also include the session info:

messages.subject: Binary Indicator Model Warning Messages
messages.subject_clean: Binary Indicator Model Warning Messages
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

As part of a simulation, I'm simulating models with binary indicators.  In a single factor model, I want to isolate the correlation between the covariate "x1" and the residual "y16_p" as well as the factor "g".  This is done after a measurement model involving only the indicators of g is obtained so that loadings can be constrained.  In the code below, I create a phantom variable for y16 and manually set the variance of g to 1.

In every sample I simulate using this procedure, I obtain a set of warnings that suggest something is wrong with the results.  I'm hoping someone can help me work through these issues which, as far as I can tell, are unique to binary indicators (the warnings were not obtained in my simulations of normally distributed indicators).

Here is the recurring set of warnings:

Warning messages:
1: In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING:
    Could not compute standard errors! The information matrix could
    not be inverted. This may be a symptom that the model is not
    identified.
2: In lav_test_satorra_bentler(lavobject = NULL, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING: could not invert information matrix needed for robust test statistic

3: In lav_object_post_check(object) :
  lavaan WARNING: some estimated ov variances are negative

Here is the code to reproduce these warnings:

## load the packages
library(lavaan)

## load the data
load("lavaan_gg.RData")

## specifying variable names to be considered "ordered"
sample.data.names <- paste0("y", 1:16)

## model specification with loadings fixed based on measurement model
s.syntax <- "\n                 \n                 g =~ (0.812)*y1 + (0.804)*y2 + (0.836)*y3 + (0.806)*y4 + (0.808)*y5 + (0.821)*y6 + (0.814)*y7 + (0.791)*y8 + \n                 (0.821)*y9 + (0.851)*y10 + (0.797)*y11 + (0.802)*y12 + (0.797)*y13 + (0.829)*y14 + (0.804)*y15 + (0.846)*y16\n                 \n                 ## phantom creation \n ## correlations \ng ~~ x1 \ny16_p =~ 1*y16 \n y16 ~~ 0*y16 \n y16_p ~~ x1 \ng ~~ 1*g \n"

## run the model
df.fit.strreg <- lavaan(s.syntax,
                        data = s.data,
                        auto.var = T,
                        auto.cov.lv.x = FALSE,

                        estimator = "WLSMV",

                        ordered = sample.data.names,
                        std.lv <http://std.lv> = FALSE)

## view the results
summary(df.fit.strreg)
standardizedSolution(df.fit.strreg)

A few observations/questions:

(1) even though the residual variance of "y16" is explicitly set to 0, the residual variance of that indicator is negative in the output
(2) The following warning message is given:
Warning message:
In cbind(c1, c2, c3, deparse.level = 0) :
  number of rows of result is not a multiple of vector length (arg 3)
I'm not sure what this means.  I haven't been able to find documentation for this warning.  To what extent does it put into question model results?
(3) Another error/warning is given in the request of standardized results.  I'm not sure how to interpret this:
Error in if (ncol(S) == 1L) { : argument is of length zero
In addition: Warning message:
In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = object@SampleStats,  :
  lavaan WARNING:
    Could not compute standard errors! The information matrix could
    not be inverted. This may be a symptom that the model is not
    identified.

messages.body_plain:
Hi all!

I'm building a structural equation model that incorporates 4 latent variables: personal lifestyle, social lifestyle, trauma score, and the DV (well-being).

Sample = 360 people.

I've included the final model below. "pl" and "sl" represent personal and social lifestyle. The moderated mediation flows from trauma to resilience (and then the interactions with pl and sl on resilience) to well-being.

There are also interactions on pl and sl with trauma in the direct pathway. Here's also a path diagram I whipped up.  <https://i.stack.imgur.com/OK4LH.jpg>

This is the full warning I receive when running the model:
Warning message:
In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING:
    Could not compute standard errors! The information matrix could
    not be inverted. This may be a symptom that the model is not
    identified.

I've used 114 DF and have 61 free parameters (model test baseline uses 147), so I'd be surprised if it's an issue of under-identification, but I also wanted to make sure that I was correctly specifying the model in Lavaan. The SEs I will compute with bootstrapping anyway; but I think this is an issue beyond merely the SEs. The fit is not good (SRMR .119), but I'd imagine that could improve with mod indices; still there's something that doesn't seem right here. Also worth noting that even if I remove the interactions on resilience score, but not the direct pathway, I still get the same warning.

I've included some data here: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1AX50DFNik30Qsyiyp6XnPMETNfVXK83r/view?usp=sharing

Thanks much!

Hello all,

I want to build a factor analysis model using Bayesian MCMC in OpenBugs. It is a nonlinear CFA model, so I cannot use the Blavaan package. The link function I use the logit. When building the model, I found that logit link has no error terms. So I wonder how should I estimate the residual variance in this case.

Traditionally the error variance for logit link is fixed to pi^2/3.However, I remember that when I used Lavaan package with MLR or WLSMV estimators, Lavaan was able to provide different residual variances for different items, not a fixed value. Thus, I want to ask how to estimate the the residual variance for logit link?

Thank you for help.

Carol

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I have a mixture of ordinal and continuous dataset with non-normality. Missing data is another problem. so I tried to use missing = "FIML" and weighted least square estimation

The R code I used:
## ordinal data
```{r}
sem70_scale[,c("giveUpDrivingNextYear_coded",
         "ClockDrawingScore")] <-
     lapply(sem70[,c("giveUpDrivingNextYear_coded",
         "ClockDrawingScore")], ordered)
```
```{r}
measurementmodel<- '
  #measurement model
  Physical_Functioning =~ b*HandStrength_avg + c*rawWalkTime
  Visual_Functioning =~ dyFarActyBoth_logMAR + depthPercep + dyContWorseEye_contrastScore_log
  Cognitive_Functioning =~ rawUFOV + rawVSA+ rawVSA+ rawVMI+ ClockDrawingScore
  Mobility =~ d*giveUpDrivingNextYear_coded + e*driverRestriction
  '
```
```{r}
fit <- cfa(model = measurementmodel, data = sem70_scale, std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE, missing = "FIML", ordered = c("giveUpDrivingNextYear_coded", "ClockDrawingScore"),
           estimator = "DWLS")
```
And the error message I received:
"lavaan ERROR: missing = "fiml" not available in the categorial setting"
and I also received:
"estimator = "DWLS" not available in missing = "fiml"

How should I fit my not normal, ordinal and continuous mixed dataset with missing data? Thanks a lot.

Dan

messages.subject: Re: Estimating Bifactor Indices (PUC, ECV, H, FD) with ordered categorical indicators (using WLSMV or ULSMV)
messages.subject_clean: Estimating Bifactor Indices (PUC, ECV, H, FD) with ordered categorical indicators (using WLSMV or ULSMV)
messages.body_plain:
> Would the equations need changes to work with ordered categorical indicators (using WLSMV or ULSMV)?  ... I'm not aware of these indices being included in any lavaan-related package (e.g. semTools).

Only the reliability() function you are already aware of, which does account for the latent-response model that is so popular with ordinal indicators.

> I hope I did not miss that. In any case, would you consider that useful or feasible in the future?

Sure, you can submit a function to semTools that returns these indices for bifactor models.  Try looking through some of the other user-contributed function's source code to see what the procedure looks like, e.g., htmt() <https://github.com/simsem/semTools/blob/master/semTools/R/htmt.R>, and please use roxygen comments in your source code.  I rely on the roxygen2 package to automate the generation of help pages, etc.  Again, looking at the source code available on GitHub will be a good guide.

https://github.com/simsem/semTools/tree/master/semTools/R

> I try my best to understand rigorously what I do, but due to my still limited knowledge on the mathematics underlying WLSMV (or ULSMV), I preferred to ask here since most members will know better.

I don't think the estimator is important.  For instance, the Green & Yang (2009) method you cited does not require DWLS or ULS to be used to obtain point estimates.  You could use pairwise or marginal MLE.  In any case, the formulas you are using only seem to rely on point estimates, so they should apply regardless of the estimator.  Of course, what the point estimates mean can vary across estimators (e.g., PML and DWLS will return point estimates interpreted in terms of latent normal variables underlying observed ordinal variables, whereas ULS and ML will treat the numeric values of ordinal categories as though they are in fact numbers on the real line).  So the indices' interpretation might be more/less valid under certain estimators than others, but their calculations should be the same.

It might be worth reaching out for guidance from the study authors, who I'm sure would be interested if someone were trying to automate their method for lavaan users.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: Benefits of using covariance variance table as input
messages.subject_clean: Benefits of using covariance variance table as input
messages.body_plain:
> would this be better than directly inputting raw data? if they have.

No, if you have raw data, there is no benefit of using summary statistics as the input instead.

> I found the model fitting results are the same.

Only when you use MLE or GLS (or maybe ULS?) without requesting any robust corrections that require the empirical distribution of the raw data, e.g., MLM(V) or MLR, (D)WLS(MV).

> What makes many studies using variance and covariance table as input instead of raw data?

Convenience and history.  Sometimes you can only access summary statistics (e.g., if you analyze a covariance matrix reported in a published article, which my students do frequently in my SEM course), which are easy to include in a paper and do not violate any privacy issues.

> Or they are identical on model fitting?

Robust ML only adjusts the SEs and test statistic for nonnormality, so the point estimates are the same as vanilla MLE.

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: Effect of mean-centering and FIML on estimates and chi-square
messages.subject_clean: Effect of mean-centering and FIML on estimates and chi-square
messages.body_plain:
> If I ignore missingness, as expected the model fit and model results are identical on both raw data and on mean-centered data

What does "ignore" mean?  If you are using the default (listwise deletion), this is not generally true (but might coincidentally be in your data), unless you centered around the mean of the complete-case data.

> However, if some observations are removed from the data set and the same model refitted using missing=”fiml”,

What observations did you remove?  Obviously not cases with missing values, if you are still using FIML.  My comment above might be relevant here, if you just drew a random subsample of data.  It should also depend on whether the variables were centered around the full-sample means or subsample means.

Pat's point is important: make sure you actually estimate the intercepts even if you centered variables.  If the mean structure is saturated, there is no point mean centering anyway.

Finally, the FIML approach will use all available data to estimate the parameters.  Complex missing-data patterns make it difficult to guess from mere sample stats what the ML-estimated mean should be, if you do want to continue mean-centering for some reason.  You could estimate the model with estimated intercepts (e.g., set int.ov.free or int.lv.free=TRUE, the former is the default in sem(), see ?lavOptions for details) using FIML, then extract the saturated-model estimated means using lavInspect(fit, "sampstat").

Some of these issues are discussed in Savalei & Yuan's (2009) article on the model-based ("Bollen-Stine") bootstrap with missing data, if you are interested:  http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/00273170903333590

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject_clean: CFA- two indicators
messages.body_plain:
> What if they are not on the same matric? It looks like they are not on the same metric.

I don't think that is really necessary.  If you fix both loadings to 1 and estimate the factor variance, the estimated factor variance should match the observed covariance between those 2 indicators (i.e., the common variance is the common variance).  The idea that fixing a loading to 1 passes the indicator's metric to the factor is a very common misunderstanding with a lot of inertia:  https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/1082-989X.7.2.210

> - Should we check the fit of the measurement models first using cfa?

That would be a good way to evaluate the fit of your measurement models, which FSR assumes is basically correct.

> - Is lavaan:::fsr() the best option for factor score regression or is it better to perform the procedure ourself with lavPredict()?

fsr() is still hidden because it needs more testing and research, but the analytical solution seems very promising.  The plausible values approach has a little more historical precedent, and is automated by semTools::plausibleValues() in combination with semTools::runMI().  The plausible values approach should be the same as fsr() when the number of "imputations" is asymptotically large.

Hi Terrence,

Thanks for the reply. This morning the problme occured again. Super frustrating. However, I found a potential solution proposed by you some time ago that seem to have worked again. For the record I post it here again. May it be of help to others as well:

It looks like you are using RStudio, which has default settings to automatically save your workspace when you shutdown RStudio, then load it automatically when you start RStudio in the same directory.  That can have unintended negative consequences, such as loading the same namespaces that were loaded before (sometimes preventing proper re-installation, or loading an irrelevant package that also has a coef method that is competing with semTools for some reason).

Click on Tools --> Global options... , and in the General tab, do 2 things:
uncheck the box that says "Restore .RData into workspace at startup
Choose "Never" in the drop-down menu next to "Save workspace to .RData on exit"
Then shut down and restart RStudio.  You can delete the (probably hidden) .RData file from your directory, if you feel like it -- it serves no purpose unless you want to save something specific, which should be in your R scripts rather than something automatic that RStudio does without asking you first.

When you have restarted RStudio, run sessionInfo() first thing to make sure nothing is attached except the base packages:

attached base packages:
[1] stats     graphics  grDevices utils     datasets  methods   base

Then run library(semTools), which will automatically load lavaan.

Best,

Dom

messages.subject: lavaan - problems with WLSMV estimator
messages.subject_clean: lavaan - problems with WLSMV estimator
messages.body_plain:
I am running a SEM using lavaan that includes 5 latent variables. Also, I have 5 regression equations (Y~...) where outcomes are manifest variables and regressors are a mix of latents and indicators.

When I use maximum likelihood estimation the model runs without problem. But when I switch to WLSMV estimation (adding the argument estimator = "WLSMV") I am finding two problems. The first problem is that the execution becomes extremely slow taking several hours to run a single model, any idea why this is happening and if there is a way to fix it?

The second problem is that when I try to fit multigroup SEMs and start constraining the model I get the following warning:
lavaan WARNING: the optimizer (NLMINB) claimed the model converged,
                but not all elements of the gradient are (near) zero;
                the optimizer may not have found a local solution
                use check.gradient = FALSE to skip this check.

Any idea what this means? what are the implications? is this a problem? how I fix it? should I simply stay with maximum likelihood?

IMPORTANT: when I remove the regressions and keep only the measurement part (the five latent variables) the function execute fast and I stop getting the warning message. Does it mean that WLSMV should not be used when the CFA becomes a SEM?

Disclaimer: I initially posted this question on stackoverflow: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/66130345/lavaan-problems-with-wlsmv-estimator?noredirect=1#comment116917595_66130345

Thanks in advance!

I'm a graduate student conducting a multilevel path analysis in lavaan and Mplus. When comparing the results between the two programs, the results are similar but not identical. It would be greatly appreciated if you had any input on whether the differences:

messages.subject: Re: Multilevel path analysis - Comparision between lavaan and Mplus
messages.subject_clean: Multilevel path analysis - Comparision between lavaan and Mplus
messages.body_plain:
> When comparing the results between the two programs, the results are similar but not identical.

Your model specifications look the same, but there are many different algorithms for obtaining ML estimates.  Mplus has 3 options for MLSEMs:
accelerated EM (EMA; the default)
regular EM
directly maximizing the observed-data log-likelihood (ODLL)
https://www.statmodel.com/HTML_UG/chapter16V8.htm
lavaan does not offer EMA (the Mplus default), so I assume you are using different algorithms.  lavaan's default is equivalent to ODLL in Mplus, although lavaan also has an EM option that is rather slower than the Mplus implementation.

https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/multilevel.html

So if you set ALGORITHM=ODLL; in Mplus, the results might more closely match those from lavaan, but there could still be small differences.  They are all ML estimates, though, and converge as N (and number of clusters) approaches infinity.

Another possibility is that you could set conditional.x=TRUE in lavaan (the default is FALSE, and only fixed.x=TRUE).  I believe Mplus conditions endogenous variables on exogenous predictors by default, but I might be wrong.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
> 1. if my indirect effect is significant does it suggest that the effect of Group on the Outcome is significantly mediated by Ability?

Yes

> 2. Do I need to run a model that tests the mediation effects in the two groups independently? Or does that just not make any sense because there would be no 'group effect' to mediate?

Right.  In a multigroup model, the effect of the grouping variable would be the difference in intercepts of your mediator (a path) and outcome (c path), and the only regression path explicitly estimated is the b path.  If the b path differs across groups, then the grouping variable is also a moderator (see Preacher et al.'s, 2007, Model 1).

I have a technical lavaan issue, but it's on a sandboxed laptop with data I can't share info about, so I'm considering this as a workaround.

I have a 7-timepoint dataset, and I believe that there is a piecewise trajectory wherein there's a steep decline in the outcome followed by a near-flat trajectory for the remainder of measurement occasions. Estimation issues cause a true piecewise model to fail, so I'm curious whether the following series of models makes sense, as I'm primarily interested in the individual differences in that initial decline (assuming the null model doesn't fit):

model1 <- '
i =~ 1*t1 + 1*t2 + 1*t3 + 1*t4 + 1*t5 + 1*t6 + 1*t7
s =~ 0*t1 + 1*t2 + 2*t3 + 2*t4 + 2*t5 + 2*t6 + 2*t7
'
fit1 <- growth(model1, data=dat) ## linear growth ending as early as possible

model2 <- '
i =~ 1*t1 + 1*t2 + 1*t3 + 1*t4 + 1*t5 + 1*t6 + 1*t7
s =~ 0*t1 + 1*t2 + 2*t3 + 3*t4 + 3*t5 + 3*t6 + 3*t7
'
fit2 <- growth(model2, data=dat) ## linear growth ending at next time point
anova(fit1, fit2) ## or nonnest2, or compare BIC or whatever

and so forth, settling on a model that does not improve in fit terms beyond the previous model. What's wrong with this conceptually? The models don't appear to be nested, which is limiting but not a huge problem. I'd much rather a different approach. I tried to linearize the model to fit the sqrt(1/x) functional form, but it doesn't work--I expect the measurement occasions are too coarse. I should probably eject from the SEM framework at this point, but it's what I'm most familiar with.

Thanks for your input!

P.S., I know that 90% of this question is more fit for a different forum, but I find this group to be more helpful than some unnamed general methods and specific methods groups.

I don't know if you want to do that (see below). Hopefully I didn't mess up the variable names. If I understand it correctly, you can model Group as an exogenous variable (1) or use a multigroup model (2). In the second case you can check if b is moderated by Group. You can shorten the syntax here and there. Maybe you can see the idea better this way (again: if I don't mix up something). CA

library(lavaan)

# Some meaningless data
set.seed(1234)
Group <- sample(c(0,1), replace=TRUE, size = 1000)
Ability <- Group * 0.5 + sqrt(0.5^2) * rnorm(1000)
ABASP_GAC <- Ability * 0.5 + sqrt(0.5^2) * rnorm(1000)
data <- cbind(Group, Ability, ABASP_GAC)

# (1)
model <- '
Ability ~ a * Group
ABASP_GAC ~ b * Ability + c * Group
ab := a * b
total := ab + c
'

fit <- sem(model, data)
parameterEstimates(fit)

# (2)
model.uncon <- '
Ability ~ c(a1, a2) * 1
ABASP_GAC ~ c(b1, b2) * Ability
ABASP_GAC ~ c(c1, c2) * 1
a := a2 - a1

messages.body_plain:
The usual default in multiple-group CFA is to constrain the latent-variable intercepts (same as means if exogenous) to zero in one group and freely estimate them in other groups. So negative values in group 2, all else being equal, indicates the means are lower than in group 1 (on a metric untethered from the original indicators). Confidence intervals including aero suggest they're not significantly lower.

So this is all quite ordinary.

A factor model with only 2 indicators is not statistically identified. I am surprised that lavaan did not turn up that diagnosis but instead produced a "subscript out of bounds" error. Perhaps, per your call to the cfa() function, the function both standardized the common factor AND fixed the first loading to 1, thus reducing the number of estimated parameters to 3, the same as the number of unique elements in the covariance matrix of the two observed variables. You could make the model identified by imposing an equality constraint on the two loadings.

messages.body_plain:
Hello

I am following the method in a published paper to perform SEM to examine a causal model built based on a theoretical framework developed by previous research.

I am confused about the method they used. The study in this paper followed  Anderson and Gerbing (1988)'s method. The baseline model first being constructed to confirm the stability of the latent variables; then they specified the causal model, which has all of the proposed paths whether they are significant or not (full model). Then the trimmed model is generated by eliminating the least non-significant path only the significant paths remaining in the model.

I understand "full model",  which seems like the proposed theoretical model, and the following trimmed model.  However, I don't understand the "baseline model" in this method. What it looks like?

I found some studies performed CFA first to test the measurement model first, then performed SEM to test the structural model.  I am unsure which method to take.

Thank you very much.
Thanks

Hi,
Thank you again for the quick reply and useful resources. I will definitely check these out.

If I have understood the concept of invariance correctly (this assumes that the models for both groups measure the same construct?), I would also assume that the models are invariant due to the fact that the same validated measures are used in both. However, this interpretation may not be correct and I have not formally tested this. My impression is that measurement invariance is usually assessed in multi-group cfa modelling as this formally tests for factors or 'constructs'?

In addition based on the following paper (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4616155/) I thought the following model might also work (based on their model 8), but was unsure about the difference with the model you proposed.

modeltest <- '

Ability ~ c(a1, a2) * 1
ABASP_GAC ~ c(b1, b2) * Ability
ABASP_GAC ~ c(c1, c2) * 1

a := a2 - a1

b := b2 - b1
ab1 := a * b1
ab2 := a * b2
intDff := ab2 - ab1
'
The model runs fine and the intDff gives the moderated mediation effect in this case (p-value is in fact the same as through the lavTestLRT).

Thank you for your help so far, if you have any thoughts on the questions above that would be amazing but I also understand that I can't just keep asking questions!
Sara

messages.subject: Re: Analogous AIC/BIC for WLSMV estimator
messages.subject_clean: Analogous AIC/BIC for WLSMV estimator
messages.body_plain:
A clarification first, AIC and BIC are not measures of parsimony. They are approximation of out-of-sample predictive accuracy, correcting for the overfitting of in-sample predictive accuracy measures (log-likelihood).
As the chi-square is calculted from LL you could theoretically do the same adjustement: chi-square + 2*K, where k is the number of parameters. But I am pretty sure this doesnt work the same way, because these were design for measures of predictive accuracy for continuous variables, so shouldnt be used with other types of estimators

As for measures of parsimony, this is a complex topic on definying parismony. I would even consider gamma-hat as better index of it. You can estimate it from the moreFitIndices function from semTools.

See these references for more details
Preacher, K. J., & Merkle, E. C. (2012). The problem of model selection uncertainty in structural equation modeling. Psychological Methods, 17, 1–14. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0026804
Preacher, Kristopher J. (2006). Quantifying parsimony in structural equation modeling. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 41(3), 227–259. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327906mbr4103_1

Yes this is cause for concern. not positive definite usually suggests you have too many factors for your data. looking at the titles it seems that there may only be a negative and positive factor. look at the correlation values--if any are close to or more than 1.00 that will cause this result.
good advice on this problem in
Chen, F., Bollen, K. A., Paxton, P., Curran, P. J., & Kirby, J. B. (2001). Improper solutions in structural equation models: Causes, consequences, and strategies. Sociological Methods & Research, 29(4), 468-508. doi:doi:10.1177/0049124101029004003

you may succeed with a bifactor model: valence on one side and act, int, dur on the other side as 2 sets of predictors for each item

messages.subject_clean: moderated mediation
messages.body_plain:
Hello together :) I am currently doing my masterthesis in psychology and have to do a moderated mediation in lavaan.

I assume that age predicts biospheric, altruistic and egoistic environmental concern and that the relationships are mediated by either self-enhanced or self-transcendet value orientation. Furthermore, the path of age on self-enhancement is moderated by Accommodative Flexibility resulting in a moderated mediation model. You can find a graphic of the model attachted.

I tried to formulate the syntax but I am very unsure whether I did this correctly (especially the moderated mediation part). Therefore, I would appreciate feedback a lot!

I am doing latent modeling.

Here is my syntax:

#Interaction term which should be double mean centered

DS <- indProd(DS, var1 = c("age"), var2 = c("af1", "af2", "af3", "af4", "af5"), match = FALSE, meanC = TRUE, residualC = FALSE, doubleMC = TRUE, namesProd = NULL)

#moderated mediation: specify model

modmedmodel03 <- '
Bio =~ EC01_01 + EC01_02 + EC01_03 + EC01_04
Alt =~ EC01_09 + EC01_10 + EC01_11 + EC01_12
Ego  =~ EC01_05 + EC01_06 + EC01_07 + EC01_08
Selftrans =~ BENE1 + BENE2 + UNI1 + UNI2 + UNI3
Selfenha =~ HED + ACH + POW1 +POW2
AccomodativeF =~ af1 + af2 + af3 + af4 + af5
interaction =~ age.af1 + age.af2 + age.af3 + age.af4 + age.af5

Bio ~~ Alt
Alt ~~ Ego
Ego ~~ Bio
Selfenha ~~ Selftrans

#direct effects
Bio ~ c1*age
Alt ~ c2*age
Ego ~ c3*age

#mediation1
Selfenha ~ a1*age
Ego ~ b1*Selfenha

#modmed 1
Selftrans ~ a2*age + w*AccomodativeF + mw*interaction
Bio ~ b2*Selftrans

#modmed 2
Alt ~ b3*Selftrans

#direct effects
direct1 := c1
direct2:= c2
direct3 := c3

# indirect effect1 (a1*b1)
ab1 := a1*b1

# indirect effect2 (a2*b2)
ab2 := a2*b2

messages.subject: Re: Little MCAR test significant
messages.subject_clean: Little MCAR test significant
messages.body_plain:
This is a bad test, doesnt actually answer what you want.
It tests if the missingness is MCAR. But if it isnt, it could be MCAR (best case scenario) or MNAR (worts case scenario)

Either way, the recommendations as basically the same, FIML or Multiple Imputation. If you have large samples with a lot of variables, they are equivalent.
If you have a model with few variables, you can add auxiliary variables to the FIML process (cfa.aux function from semTools), or you can add more variables to the imputation process.
The multiple imputation can be done with he runMI function from semTools

messages.subject: Re: Anderson and Gerbing (1988)'s method What is baseline model
messages.subject_clean: Anderson and Gerbing (1988)'s method What is baseline model
messages.body_plain:
> I found some studies performed CFA first to test the measurement model first, then performed SEM to test the structural model.

That is what Anderson & Gerbing (1988) advocated.  The idea is that the latent structure is unconstrained in a CFA, analogous to the saturated "h1" model that simply estimates all covariances among observed variables.  Just as a model's chi-squared is a LRT that compares the theoretical "h0" model to the saturated h1 model, the 2-step approach tries to achieve the same by starting with a CFA (saturated latent spaces: freely estimate all covariances) and comparing an SEM with constraints on the latent structure using a LRT (chi-squared difference).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Latent Growth Curve Model
messages.subject_clean: Latent Growth Curve Model
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I hope you are doing well. I have another question :)
To recapitalize:
I established longitudinal strong measurement invariance for three time points of boredom
I added growth parameters (intercept and slope) to the strong boredom model to investigate the trajectories of boredom
I added health variables to this model that were raised at time point 3 to explore if changes in boredom across the three time points were correlatively linked with those variables
The results of 3. show that stronger increases of boredom (slope) are linked with two health variables, which I want to report.
But I am wondering – since at 2. the variance of this slope is not significantly different from zero (tau2 = .864, p = .055) – does it even make sense to explain the variance of the slope in 3.? On the other hand, the constraints of the strong model are limiting the variance.

I attached the results and will add my R script in the next post. I am looking forward to hearing your thoughts.

Thanks,
Manuel

# * 2.3 Strong Invariance -------------------------------------------------

# model specification (additional constraints on manifest intercepts)
strong_boredom <- '
# measurement model
boredom_0 =~ lambda1*bos1_0 + lambda2*bos2_0 + lambda3*bos3_0 + lambda4*bos4_0 + lambda5*bos5_0 + lambda6*bos6_0
boredom_1 =~ lambda1*bos1_1 + lambda2*bos2_1 + lambda3*bos3_1 + lambda4*bos4_1 + lambda5*bos5_1 + lambda6*bos6_1
boredom_2 =~ lambda1*bos1_2 + lambda2*bos2_2 + lambda3*bos3_2 + lambda4*bos4_2 + lambda5*bos5_2 + lambda6*bos6_2

# intercepts
bos1_0 ~ i1*1
bos2_0 ~ i2*1
bos3_0 ~ i3*1
bos4_0 ~ i4*1
bos5_0 ~ i5*1
bos6_0 ~ i6*1
bos1_1 ~ i1*1
bos2_1 ~ i2*1
bos3_1 ~ i3*1
bos4_1 ~ i4*1
bos5_1 ~ i5*1
bos6_1 ~ i6*1
bos1_2 ~ i1*1
bos2_2 ~ i2*1
bos3_2 ~ i3*1
bos4_2 ~ i4*1
bos5_2 ~ i5*1
bos6_2 ~ i6*1

# unique variances and covariances
bos1_0 ~~ bos1_0
bos2_0 ~~ bos2_0
bos3_0 ~~ bos3_0
bos4_0 ~~ bos4_0
bos5_0 ~~ bos5_0
bos6_0 ~~ bos6_0
bos1_1 ~~ bos1_1
bos2_1 ~~ bos2_1
bos3_1 ~~ bos3_1
bos4_1 ~~ bos4_1
bos5_1 ~~ bos5_1
bos6_1 ~~ bos6_1
bos1_2 ~~ bos1_2
bos2_2 ~~ bos2_2
bos3_2 ~~ bos3_2
bos4_2 ~~ bos4_2
bos5_2 ~~ bos5_2
bos6_2 ~~ bos6_2
bos1_0 ~~ bos1_1 + bos1_2
bos1_1 ~~ bos1_2
bos2_0 ~~ bos2_1 + bos2_2
bos2_1 ~~ bos2_2
bos3_0 ~~ bos3_1 + bos3_2

bos5_0 ~~ bos5_1 + bos5_2

bos6_1 ~~ bos6_2

# latent variables means
boredom_0 ~ 0*1
boredom_1 ~ NA*1
boredom_2 ~ NA*1

# latent variables variances and covariances
boredom_0 ~~ 1*boredom_0
boredom_1 ~~ NA*boredom_1
boredom_2 ~~ NA*boredom_2
'

# model estimation
fit_strong_boredom <- lavaan::cfa(strong_boredom, data=df1, missing="FIML", estimator="MLR", std.lv <http://std.lv>=T)
summary(fit_strong_boredom, fit.measures=T, standardized=T)

# further insights
lavaan::modindices(fit_strong_boredom, sort.=T)
lavaan::lavTestScore(fit_strong_boredom, epc=T)

modelcomparison

Pat

messages.body_plain:
Hi, I am running many baseline CFA models using lavCor function (I needed many covariance matrices dealing with missing data by FIML). In some cases (a subset of items or participants), there is no variance in an item, and thus the whole function fails.
Usually, in CFA or SEM functions, it is not any problem to manually delete an item and then proceed with the rest of the data. Moreover, it is generally better to manually control this data exclusion, but it is still boring. But now, my whole function fails. I have manually added a control, so I have solved the problem, but have you ever think about adding some parameter to the lavaan function, like, e.g., drop.zero.variance.ov = TRUE? This would help very much.
Best,
Hynek

messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I've fitted a multi-group mediation model with three parallel mediators and three covariates.
The model successfully converged and provides a summary just fine.
However, when I attempt to simulate the data using simulateData or using sim in the package simsem, I get the following error:

Error in lavaanify(model = model, meanstructure = meanstructure, int.ov.free = int.ov.free,  :
  lavaan ERROR: wrong number of arguments in modifier (M1YDirectA,M1YDirectB,M1YDirectC,M1YDirectD) of element Y~M1

However, the number of modifiers I've included is equal to the number of groups I have, which is 4.

I saw a previous post where someone had the same issue and the suggestion was to try it as a multilevel model. Is there a different way to do this or perhaps my construction of the model is incorrect? I constructed the model in two different ways because I am unsure about whether each indirect and total effect needed to have all four modifiers.

 Thank you for your help!

Version 1

See below:

modelH2a <- '
##DIRECT EFFECT
Y ~ c(M1YDirectA, M1YDirectB, M1YDirectC, M1YDirectD)*M1 + c(M2YDirectA, M2YDirectB, M2YDirectC, M2YDirectD)*M2 + c(M3YDirectA, M3YDirectB, M3YDirectC, M3YDirectD)*M3 + c(X1YDirectA, X1YDirectB, X1YDirectC, X1YDirectD)*X1 + c(X2YDirectA, X2YDirectB, X2YDirectC, X2YDirectD)*X2 + c(X3YDirectA, X3YDirectB, X3YDirectC, X3YDirectD)*X3 + c(X4YDirectA, X4YDirectB, X4YDirectC, X4YDirectD)*X4

##MEDIATORS
M1 ~ c(X1M1a, X1M1b, X1M1c, X1M1d)*X1 + c(X2M1a, X2M1b, X2M1c, X2M1d)*X2 + c(X3M1a, X3M1b, X3M1c, X3M1d)*X3 + c(X4M1a, X4M1b, X4M1c, X4M1d)*X4
M2 ~ c(X1M2a, X1M2b, X1M2c, X1M2d)*X1 + c(X2M2a, X2M2b, X2M2c, X2M2d)*X2 + c(X3M2a, X3M2b, X3M2c, X3M2d)*X3 + c(X4M2a, X4M2b, X4M2c, X4M2d)*X4
M3 ~ c(X1M3a, X1M3b, X1M3c, X1M3d)*X1 + c(X2M3a, X2M3b, X2M3c, X2M3d)*X2 + c(X3M3a, X3M3b, X3M3c, X3M3d)*X3 + c(X4M3a, X4M3b, X4M3c, X4M3d)*X4

##INDIRECT EFFECTS
###X1 -> Y via M1, M2, M3
abX1M1a := (X1M1a*M1YDirectA)
abX1M1b := (X1M1b*M1YDirectB)
abX1M1c := (X1M1c*M1YDirectC)
abX1M1d := (X1M1d*M1YDirectD)

abX1M2a := (X1M2a*M2YDirectA)
abX1M2b := (X1M2b*M2YDirectB)
abX1M2c := (X1M2c*M2YDirectC)
abX1M2d := (X1M2d*M2YDirectD)

abX1M3a := (X1M3a*M3YDirectA)
abX1M3b := (X1M3b*M3YDirectB)
abX1M3c := (X1M3c*M3YDirectC)
abX1M3d := (X1M3d*M3YDirectD)

##TOTAL EFFECTS
totalX1A := X1YDirectA + (X1M1a*M1YDirectA) + (X1M2a*M2YDirectA) + (X1M3a*M3YDirectA)
totalX1B := X1YDirectB + (X1M1b*M1YDirectB) + (X1M2b*M2YDirectB) + (X1M3b*M3YDirectB)
totalX1C := X1YDirectC + (X1M1c*M1YDirectC) + (X1M2c*M2YDirectC) + (X1M3c*M3YDirectC)
totalX1D := X1YDirectD + (X1M1d*M1YDirectD) + (X1M2d*M2YDirectD) + (X1M3d*M3YDirectD)'

Version 2
modelH2c <- '
##DIRECT EFFECT
Y ~ c(M1YDirectA, M1YDirectB, M1YDirectC, M1YDirectD)*M1 + c(M2YDirectA, M2YDirectB, M2YDirectC, M2YDirectD)*M2 + c(M3YDirectA, M3YDirectB, M3YDirectC, M3YDirectD)*M3 + c(X1YDirectA, X1YDirectB, X1YDirectC, X1YDirectD)*X1 + c(X2YDirectA, X2YDirectB, X2YDirectC, X2YDirectD)*X2 + c(X3YDirectA, X3YDirectB, X3YDirectC, X3YDirectD)*X3 + c(X4YDirectA, X4YDirectB, X4YDirectC, X4YDirectD)*X4

##MEDIATORS
M1 ~ c(X1M1a, X1M1b, X1M1c, X1M1d)*X1 + c(X2M1a, X2M1b, X2M1c, X2M1d)*X2 + c(X3M1a, X3M1b, X3M1c, X3M1d)*X3 + c(X4M1a, X4M1b, X4M1c, X4M1d)*X4
M2 ~ c(X1M2a, X1M2b, X1M2c, X1M2d)*X1 + c(X2M2a, X2M2b, X2M2c, X2M2d)*X2 + c(X3M2a, X3M2b, X3M2c, X3M2d)*X3 + c(X4M2a, X4M2b, X4M2c, X4M2d)*X4
M3 ~ c(X1M3a, X1M3b, X1M3c, X1M3d)*X1 + c(X2M3a, X2M3b, X2M3c, X2M3d)*X2 + c(X3M3a, X3M3b, X3M3c, X3M3d)*X3 + c(X4M3a, X4M3b, X4M3c, X4M3d)*X4

##INDIRECT EFFECTS
###X1 -> Y via M1, M2, M3

abM1 := (c(X1M1a, X1M1b, X1M1c, X1M1d)*X1) * (c(M1YDirectA, M1YDirectB, M1YDirectC, M1YDirectD)*M1)
abM2 := (c(X1M2a, X1M2b, X1M2c, X1M2d)*X1) * (c(M2YDirectA, M2YDirectB, M2YDirectC, M2YDirectD)*M2)
abM3 := (c(X1M3a, X1M3b, X1M3c, X1M3d)*X1) * (c(M3YDirectA, M3YDirectB, M3YDirectC, M3YDirectD)*M3)

##TOTAL EFFECTS
totalX1 := (c(X1YDirectA, X1YDirectB, X1YDirectC, X1YDirectD)*X1) + abM1 + abM2 + abM3'

messages.subject: Re: Using bootstrapLavaan with Modification Indices
messages.subject_clean: Using bootstrapLavaan with Modification Indices
messages.body_plain:
When you use SNOW (available on all platforms) instead of multicore (not available on Windows), you need to make sure any relevant objects are available in the workspace that gets created on the worker nodes. At a minimum, you need to load the lavaan library to use its functions.  Also, in an example using only 2 bootstrap samples, no need to use more than 2 CPUs.

example(cfa)
bootstrapLavaan(fit, R=2, type="ordinary",
                FUN = function(x) {library(lavaan) ; modificationindices(x,op="=~")$mi},
                parallel="snow", ncpus = 2)

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
> Do you have any arguments against users (or reviewers) why I should predict this slope anyways?

The fixed effect of an exogenous predictor on the latent slope might be (significantly) nonzero, even if the variance of random effects around that latent slope is not (significantly) different from zero.

In a different but related situation:
I have fitted a model whose chi-squared is not significant, yet when I freed a parameter and conducted the chi-squared different test, the less restricted model fit significantly better.

> And is it common to report the variance including its p-value if I want to report the results of 3.?

Not sure about what is common, but you can do so.  THE ML estimator in lavaan does not (by default) restrict variances to be non-negative, so their sampling distributions are in fact asymptotically normal and can include negative values (particularly in smaller samples, especially when the true parameter is not substantially larger than zero relative to its sampling error).  ML estimates of variances will have non-normal sampling distributions only when using constrained estimation to guarantee non-negative estimates (e.g., the default in multilevel modeling software).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: bootstrapping with missing data
messages.subject_clean: bootstrapping with missing data
messages.body_plain:
> please advise if there are alternative ways where I could obtain yuan-bootstrapped CFI/RMSEA for path model with missing data.

I don't know of a software implementation of the YHY bootstrap, but semTools::bsBootMiss() implements the model-based ("Bollen-Stine") bootstrap, generalized by Savalei & Yuan (2009) for missing data.  By default, it will return the bootstrapped chi-squared test with p value, but you can request bootSamplesOnly=TRUE to obtain the bootstrap samples from the transformed data (i.e., consistent with H0), and with those use lavaanList() to fit the model to each and save the fit indices.  Not sure that is what you want, though.

Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject_clean: Problem in converging? lavaan 0.6-6 did NOT end normally after 416 iterations
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I would be very grateful if you could help me to find the problem with my model. Initially, I have used 2 second-level factors (LM and Connect), each with four latent constructs, and one 1st level factor to conduct mediation analysis. Following my successful attempt, I have decided to use all factors as first-order factors to check my theory. I am attaching a rather ugly looking handwritten piece for the reference (many apologies for that).

Unfortunately, the model did not converge with the following famous warning :
"lavaan 0.6-6 did NOT end normally after 416 iterations
** WARNING ** Estimates below are most likely unreliable"

Just to clarify: no missing values, n>800. The fit indices of the model with the 2nd order variables are the following: χ2/df = 2.18, p < .001, CFI = .962, TLI = .959, RMSEA = .037, SRMR = .40.

Please, advise me whether there is something wrong with my syntax.

mediation.model.1levelonly <- "
##### LM
                PERC_Attention=~ PERC3 + PERC4 + PERC2
               PERC_Relevance =~ PERC7 + PERC5 + PERC6
               PERC_Confidence =~ PERC10 + PERC11 + PERC9
               PERC_Satisfaction =~ PERC14 + PERC13 + PERC15
##### SKL
               SKL =~ SKL1 + SKL2 + SKL3 + SKL5 + SKL7 + SKL9 + SKL11 + SKL13 + SKL16
##### connect
               comf.sub =~  COLLAB3 + COLLAB4 +COLLAB6 +COLLAB7
               comm.sub =~ COLLAB10 + COLLAB11 + COLLAB12 + COLLAB13
               facil.sub =~ COLLAB15 + COLLAB16 + COLLAB17 + COLLAB18
               inter.sub =~ COLLAB22 + COLLAB23 + COLLAB24
##### measurement model
                SKL ~ d1*PERC_Attention + d2*PERC_Relevance + d3*PERC_Confidence + d4*PERC_Satisfaction
                SKL ~ b1*comf.sub + b2*comm.sub + b3*facil.sub + b4*inter.sub

                comf.sub ~ a1*PERC_Attention + r1*PERC_Relevance + c1*PERC_Confidence + s1*PERC_Satisfaction
                comm.sub ~ a2*PERC_Attention + r2*PERC_Relevance + c2*PERC_Confidence + s2*PERC_Satisfaction
                facil.sub ~ a3*PERC_Attention + r3*PERC_Relevance + c3*PERC_Confidence + s3*PERC_Satisfaction
                inter.sub ~ a4*PERC_Attention + r4*PERC_Relevance + c4*PERC_Confidence + s4*PERC_Satisfaction

##### structural model

ind1:= a1*b1
ind2:=a2*b2
ind3:= a3*b3
ind4:=a4*b4

ind5:= r1*b1
ind6:=r2*b2
ind7:= r3*b3
ind8:= r4*b4

ind9:=c1*b1
ind10:=c2*b2
ind11:=c3*b3
ind12:=c4*b4

ind13:= s1*b1
ind14:=s2*b2
ind15:=s3*b3
ind16:=s4*b4

dir1:= d1
dir2:= d2
dir3:= d3
dir4:= d4"

FULL_MODEL.1level<-sem(mediation.model.1levelonly, data=MODEL_MEDIATION_NOOUTLIERS,  estimator="MLR", missing="FIML")
summary(FULL_MODEL.1level, fit.measures=TRUE, rsquare=TRUE, standardized=TRUE)

Many thanks in advance.
Archie

I hope you are very well.

I am trying to evaluate measurement invariance for a psychological scale, but I receive an error message. The instrument is a seven-point Likert scale and the dataset consists of 1721 subjects. I already check for errors in the dataset, but none was found. Here is the code and the error message I get:

Hi Prof. Jorgensen,

Thank you so much for your prompt advice!

I have one additional question -- when we ask for se="boot", bootstrap=1000 with sem(), do we automatically get bootstrapped coefficients in the output or do we need to use the FUN="coef" in bootstrapLavaan () to get them? If I have to use the "FUN="coef",  I believe I have to remove the se="boot"  from the sem() and run another model because I received an error message when I tried to use the same model:  lavaan ERROR: se == "bootstrap"; please refit model with another option for "se"
Please advise if this is correct or not.

My syntax:
fit< -- sem(model1, data=dataset,missing = "FIML", estimator="ML", se="boot", bootstrap=1000, std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE).  ##get bootstrapped standard error
confit <--parameterEstimates(fit, level=0.95, boot.ci.type="bca.simple") ##get bootstrapped confidence interval
bootest <--bootstrapLavaan(model1, R = 1000L, type = "ordinary", verbose = FALSE, FUN = "coef", parallel = c("no", "multicore"), ncpus = 1L) ##get bootstrapped coefficients?

I am in the process of writing my thesis, so your advice is great appreciated!!

-- Tracy

On Wednesday, 24 February 2021 at 22:35:47 UTC-5 Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> >
> > please advise if there are alternative ways where I could obtain yuan-bootstrapped CFI/RMSEA for path model with missing data.
>
> I don't know of a software implementation of the YHY bootstrap, but semTools::bsBootMiss() implements the model-based ("Bollen-Stine") bootstrap, generalized by Savalei & Yuan (2009) for missing data.  By default, it will return the bootstrapped chi-squared test with p value, but you can request bootSamplesOnly=TRUE to obtain the bootstrap samples from the transformed data (i.e., consistent with H0), and with those use lavaanList() to fit the model to each and save the fit indices.  Not sure that is what you want, though.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

If you only present the error message, without the syntax that produce it, its really hard for us to figure out what is the problem. We are guessing here what could be the problem, for example did you use n as the argument for sample size? because the argument for sample size sample.nobs.
Please share the full code that produce the errors

Also, its not a "bug" that simsem doesnt work the same for multiple groups with the lavaan syntax. Its a difference in features given how the user wants to use it

The main difference is that you have to create your full population first with simulatedata, like 10000 subjects per group first, then you pass this full population to simsem instead of a syntax. Then you have an analysis syntax, and a population data set for the simsem

Error in names(Data) <- var.names :
  'names' attribute [9] must be the same length as the vector [5]

Here is the model syntax as well, in case something in there is causing the issue. It is supposed to be a multigroup mediation model with three parallel mediators and three control variables (X2,X3,X4). I am eternally grateful for your help. Thank you.

modelH2a <- '
##DIRECT EFFECT
Y ~ c(M1YDirectA, M1YDirectB, M1YDirectC, M1YDirectD)*M1 + c(M2YDirectA, M2YDirectB, M2YDirectC, M2YDirectD)*M2 + c(M3YDirectA, M3YDirectB, M3YDirectC, M3YDirectD)*M3 + c(X1YDirectA, X1YDirectB, X1YDirectC, X1YDirectD)*X1 + c(X2YDirectA, X2YDirectB, X2YDirectC, X2YDirectD)*X2 + c(X3YDirectA, X3YDirectB, X3YDirectC, X3YDirectD)*X3 + c(X4YDirectA, X4YDirectB, X4YDirectC, X4YDirectD)*X4

##MEDIATORS
M1 ~ c(X1M1a, X1M1b, X1M1c, X1M1d)*X1 + c(X2M1a, X2M1b, X2M1c, X2M1d)*X2 + c(X3M1a, X3M1b, X3M1c, X3M1d)*X3 + c(X4M1a, X4M1b, X4M1c, X4M1d)*X4
M2 ~ c(X1M2a, X1M2b, X1M2c, X1M2d)*X1 + c(X2M2a, X2M2b, X2M2c, X2M2d)*X2 + c(X3M2a, X3M2b, X3M2c, X3M2d)*X3 + c(X4M2a, X4M2b, X4M2c, X4M2d)*X4
M3 ~ c(X1M3a, X1M3b, X1M3c, X1M3d)*X1 + c(X2M3a, X2M3b, X2M3c, X2M3d)*X2 + c(X3M3a, X3M3b, X3M3c, X3M3d)*X3 + c(X4M3a, X4M3b, X4M3c, X4M3d)*X4

##INDIRECT EFFECTS
###X1 -> Y via M1, M2, M3
abX1M1a := (X1M1a*M1YDirectA)
abX1M1b := (X1M1b*M1YDirectB)
abX1M1c := (X1M1c*M1YDirectC)
abX1M1d := (X1M1d*M1YDirectD)

abX1M2a := (X1M2a*M2YDirectA)
abX1M2b := (X1M2b*M2YDirectB)
abX1M2c := (X1M2c*M2YDirectC)
abX1M2d := (X1M2d*M2YDirectD)

abX1M3a := (X1M3a*M3YDirectA)
abX1M3b := (X1M3b*M3YDirectB)
abX1M3c := (X1M3c*M3YDirectC)
abX1M3d := (X1M3d*M3YDirectD)

##TOTAL EFFECTS
totalX1A := X1YDirectA + (X1M1a*M1YDirectA) + (X1M2a*M2YDirectA) + (X1M3a*M3YDirectA)
totalX1B := X1YDirectB + (X1M1b*M1YDirectB) + (X1M2b*M2YDirectB) + (X1M3b*M3YDirectB)
totalX1C := X1YDirectC + (X1M1c*M1YDirectC) + (X1M2c*M2YDirectC) + (X1M3c*M3YDirectC)
totalX1D := X1YDirectD + (X1M1d*M1YDirectD) + (X1M2d*M2YDirectD) + (X1M3d*M3YDirectD)'

fitH2a <- sem(modelH2a, data = PEB1, ordered= c("Y"), group = "Z")

messages.body_plain:
Ok, the problem was more basic. You dont need the delta argument, it is only for categorical data.

The porblem is that you created syntax for multiple groups but didnt specify group in the cfa function. You can use either the MLM or MLR estimators for robust SE and fit indices. You can use AIC and those for non-nested model comparison. But these models are nested, you can use the LRT methods too. You can use the compare function from semTools to show chi-square and other fit indices.
Also, for non nested models you can use the nonnest2 package

sex.fit.config <- cfa(sex.model.config, data = mydata, estimator = "MLM",  group="sex", missing="fiml")

sex.fit.config <- cfa(sex.model.metric, data = mydata, estimator = "MLM",  group="sex" , missing="fiml"  )

sex.fit.config <- cfa(sex.model.scalar, data = mydata, estimator = "MLM",  group="sex" , missing="fiml" )

Terrence Jorgensen <tjorge...@gmail.com> 于2021年2月22日周一 下午4:00写道：

> > I found some studies performed CFA first to test the measurement model first, then performed SEM to test the structural model.
>
> That is what Anderson & Gerbing (1988) advocated.  The idea is that the latent structure is unconstrained in a CFA, analogous to the saturated "h1" model that simply estimates all covariances among observed variables.  Just as a model's chi-squared is a LRT that compares the theoretical "h0" model to the saturated h1 model, the 2-step approach tries to achieve the same by starting with a CFA (saturated latent spaces: freely estimate all covariances) and comparing an SEM with constraints on the latent structure using a LRT (chi-squared difference).
>

> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

mod_meas <- '
  ## latent variable definitions (CFA)
  # The "=~" can be read as "is identified by"
  HOME_t1 =~ accept_t1 + variety_t1 + acStim_t1
  HOME_t2 =~ accept_t2 + variety_t2 + acStim_t2

  Fadhd_t1 =~ adhd_t1
  Fadhd_t2 =~ adhd_t2

  ## covariances
  #HOME_t1 ~~ HOME_t2 + Fadhd_t1 + Fadhd_t2
  #HOME_t2 ~~ Fadhd_t1 + Fadhd_t2
  #Fadhd_t1 ~~ Fadhd_t2
'

fit_meas <- cfa(mod_meas, data = adhd_home_env)
modificationIndices(fit_meas)

Works fine for me. I don't think you need to specify the covariances. The CFA function does that by default. Even if you do, it still works.

messages.body_plain:
This turns into a combination of data manipulation and missing data. Try searching on "cohort sequential" or "accelerated longitudinal" design. That should get you in the right direction.

On Sat, Feb 27, 2021 at 9:45 AM Michal Levinsky <michal....@mail.huji.ac.il> wrote:

>
>
> I performed a Latent Growth Model analysis in Lavaan based on six time-points (waves), which looked like this:
>
> model.mob2 <- '
>   # intercept and slope with fixed coefficients
>   i =~ 1*Y_1 + 1*Y_2 + 1*Y_3 + 1*Y_4+ 1*Y_5 + 1*Y_6
>   s =~ 1*Y_1 + 2*Y_2 + 3*Y_3 + 4*Y_4+ 5*Y_5 + 6*Y_6
>
>   # regressions
>   i ~ x + z + r + age
>   s ~ x + z + r + age
>   '
> I was asked to run an age-based model, rather than the wave-based model. In addition,  to include a quadratic age effect or examine the possibility of pivot points at which the rate of decline changes (spline or two-slope models).

> I did not find any source on the subject. I would appreciate some guidance, how to change the code, and how to understand its interpretation.
